newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo says Menem gov't fears businessman Yabran.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo says Menem gov't fears businessman Yabran.

text.p: Former Argentine economy minister Domingo Cavallo, continuing a campaign against graft, accused the Peronist government Monday of aiding out of fear a businessman whom he alleges heads a crime syndicate.

Cavallo's latest outburst against postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran was in response to Economy Minister Roque Fernandez's assurances that a decree to privatize the state post office does not include an "anti-Yabran clause."

The full extent of Yabran's business empire is not clear, but Cavallo says he is building a monopoly in the deregulated postal business for criminal ends, as well as his interests in the delivery of official documents and in private security.

"I am convinced that if Yabran, who heads a mafia, gets away with it with the clear support of the government, that means it is clear that what is happening is a clear strategy planned jointly by the government and Yabran," said Cavallo.
Cavallo, who was fired by President Carlos Menem last July, denounced Yabran in a detailed address to Congress in August 1995 which sparked legal action by the businessman.
Since then, Yabran through his spokesman has repeatedly denied Cavallo's charges. And last week, he gave his first press interview in years.
In the interview, published by Clarin newspaper on Sunday, Yabran said: "Don't call me a mobster."
Yabran declined to disclose his wealth but did say he paid $2 million in personal taxes last year and his postal firm OCASA $40 million. He lashed out at Cavallo, telling Clarin:
"This gentleman Cavallo, if he continues like this he will become a peril for all society, not just me."

Yabran also alleged that the postal privatization decree included an "anti-Yabran clause" to stop him seeking a stake. But Fernandez told reporters Sunday: "There is no anti-Yabran clause but neither is there a pro-Yabran clause."
But Cavallo, running for Congress this year as an independent, has stepped up his campaign ahead of an imminent presidential decree to privatize the state post office.
"Unfortunately I believe President Menem and other senior officials are afraid of Yabran," said Cavallo.

Congress wants Yabran summoned to a twin-house committee on security this week to explain his security interests. One poll showed over 80 percent disapproval of Peronist deputies' moves last week to block his appearance.
